---
title: "Field guide: outputs and tools"
description: "How generated text becomes data, evidence or an action request"
---

A model normally returns text. Research software often needs to parse that text, validate its structure and decide what—if anything—to do with it.

<div class="concept-flow"><div><strong>Raw return</strong><span>text from the model</span></div><div><strong>Parsing</strong><span>turn text into a Python object</span></div><div><strong>Structural check</strong><span>test fields and types</span></div><div><strong>Substantive check</strong><span>compare with evidence</span></div></div>

## Plain text and JSON {#plain-text-json}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Week 3</span>

**In plain English.** Plain text is an unstructured string. JSON is a text format for representing objects such as dictionaries and lists.

```python
plain_text = "The theme is solidarity."
json_text = '{"theme": "solidarity", "evidence_id": "e01"}'
print(type(plain_text))
print(type(json_text))
```

<div class="glossary-output">&lt;class 'str'&gt;
&lt;class 'str'&gt;</div>

**Common confusion.** JSON returned by a model is still a Python string until we parse it.

## Parsing {#parsing}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Week 3</span>

**In plain English.** Parsing reads text according to a known format and creates a structured Python object.

```python
import json

raw_output = '{"theme": "solidarity", "evidence_id": "e01"}'
parsed_output = json.loads(raw_output)
print(type(parsed_output))
print(parsed_output["evidence_id"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">&lt;class 'dict'&gt;
e01</div>

**Input → operation → output.** `json.loads(...)` receives a string and returns a dictionary. Square brackets retrieve one value.

**Why it matters.** Parsing makes fields accessible to code. It does not tell us whether the proposed theme or citation is correct.

## Schema {#schema}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 3 and 7</span>

**In plain English.** A schema describes the fields, types and requirements an output should satisfy.

```python
schema = {
    "required": ["label", "confidence"],
    "types": {"label": "string", "confidence": "number"},
}
print(schema["required"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">['label', 'confidence']</div>

**Why it matters.** A schema makes an output contract explicit. It is useful for consistent data collection but does not define the construct being measured.

## Structured output and constrained decoding {#structured-output}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 3 and 7</span>

**In plain English.** Structured output asks the model to return a specified form. Some systems use constrained decoding to restrict generation so the return conforms to a grammar or schema.

```python
requested_shape = {
    "label": "SUPPORT | OPPOSE | UNCLEAR",
    "reason": "one short string",
}
model_return = {"label": "SUPPORT", "reason": "The speaker endorses the proposal."}
print(model_return.keys() == requested_shape.keys())
```

<div class="glossary-output">True</div>

**Common confusion.** Matching the requested keys is structural success. Whether `SUPPORT` is the right label is a separate measurement question.

See the [Ollama structured-output documentation](https://docs.ollama.com/capabilities/structured-outputs) for a live route-specific implementation.

## Structural and substantive validation {#validation}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 2–13</span>

**In plain English.** Structural validation checks whether data have the expected form. Substantive validation checks whether the resulting claim, label or prediction is supported.

```python
result = {"label": "SUPPORT", "evidence_id": "missing-id"}
known_ids = ["e01", "e02"]

structure_ok = set(result) == {"label", "evidence_id"}
evidence_exists = result["evidence_id"] in known_ids
print(structure_ok, evidence_exists)
```

<div class="glossary-output">True False</div>

**Why it matters.** The dictionary is structurally complete while its citation fails a basic source check.

## Tool definition, call and result {#tool-calling}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Week 11</span>

**In plain English.** A tool definition tells a model what operation is available and what arguments it accepts. A tool call is the model's request to use it. A tool result is the value returned by the surrounding program.

```python
tool_definition = {"name": "find_excerpt", "argument": "excerpt_id"}
tool_call = {"name": "find_excerpt", "arguments": {"excerpt_id": "e02"}}
corpus = {"e02": "I accepted help but did not attend meetings."}
tool_result = corpus[tool_call["arguments"]["excerpt_id"]]
print(tool_result)
```

<div class="glossary-output">I accepted help but did not attend meetings.</div>

**Input → operation → output.** The model-style call supplies an ID. Ordinary Python retrieves the corresponding source text. The model does not execute arbitrary Python here.

**Why it matters.** Tool use introduces another operation and another possible failure between a prompt and a final claim.

## Multimodal input {#multimodal-input}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Week 4</span>

**In plain English.** A multimodal request contains more than one kind of input, such as text and an image.

```python
content = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Describe only visible changes."},
    {"type": "image", "path": "frame_02.png"},
]
print([item["type"] for item in content])
```

<div class="glossary-output">['text', 'image']</div>

**Why it matters.** The text instruction and image are both part of the research instrument. A model may also rely on prior visual associations that were not supplied in the image.

## Speech-to-text and text-to-speech {#speech-interfaces}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Week 6</span>

**In plain English.** Speech-to-text, or STT, converts audio into text. Text-to-speech, or TTS, turns text into generated audio. Neither is the interviewing model itself.

```python
audio_file = "participant_answer.wav"
transcript = "The rent increase changed who could stay."
follow_up = "What happened next?"
spoken_output_file = "follow_up.wav"
print(audio_file, "→", transcript)
print(follow_up, "→", spoken_output_file)
```

<div class="glossary-output">participant_answer.wav → The rent increase changed who could stay.
What happened next? → follow_up.wav</div>

**Why it matters.** Transcription errors and synthetic voice characteristics become part of the research encounter and need separate evaluation.

## Log probabilities {#log-probabilities}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Model audits</span>

**In plain English.** A log probability is a logarithmic representation of the probability the model assigned to a candidate token. Some APIs expose these values.

```python
import math

log_probability = -0.36
probability = math.exp(log_probability)
print(round(probability, 2))
```

<div class="glossary-output">0.70</div>

**Why it matters.** Token probability can describe uncertainty at a generation step. It is not automatically calibrated confidence in the substantive correctness of an answer.

## Function parameter and named argument {#function-parameter}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Weeks 5 and 9</span>

**In plain English.** A parameter is a name in a function definition. An argument is the value supplied when the function is called. Named arguments make the relationship visible.

```python
def make_request(temperature):
    return {"temperature": temperature}

request = make_request(temperature=0.2)
print(request)
```

<div class="glossary-output">{'temperature': 0.2}</div>

**Why it matters.** Model settings such as `temperature` are ordinary values passed into client functions. They should be explicit rather than hidden inside unexplained code.
